newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African apartheid generals face judgment day.
newsitem.headline: S.African apartheid generals face judgment day.

text.p: Judgment day began on Friday for Magnus Malan, the former South African defence minister on trial for the massacre of 13 blacks nine years ago in the "dirty war" against foes of apartheid.

Malan, the most senior apartheid-era leader to be tried for atrocities, appeared with nine co-defendants at court in the Indian Ocean city of Durban on Friday, apparently buoyed by the acquittal of six others in the trial a day earlier.
Those still to be judged included a top Inkatha official, three generals, two majors, a vice-admiral, a brigadier and a senior policeman.

Thursday's acquittals immediately sparked speculation that Malan would also walk free -- a verdict which some political analysts said would further damage the public's shaky faith in the South African justice system.
The six cleared on Thursday were policemen in the KwaZulu black homeland run by Inkatha Freedom Party leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi until it was scrapped after all-race elections in April 1994.

Supreme court judge Jan Hugo found them not guilty of any of the charges brought against them by the state, which was trying to prove they were responsible for the 1987 death squad killing of 13 people in KwaMakutha near the port of Durban.
Inkatha hailed their acquittal as "a triumph of justice".
"The state should in future be more prudent and cautious before embarking on prosecutions which are widely perceived to have high-level political connotations," it said in a statement.
But the rival African National Congress of President Nelson Mandela called the verdict a travesty.

"In the eyes of the our people, the prosecution team failed them. This will have far reaching consequences. It is doubtful whether our people will ever have confidence in the judicial system if it remains the same," the ANC said.

Senior members of the movement have previously lamented the fact that most of South Africa's judges are white men appointed during the apartheid era, and have accused some of them of administering racially-biased justice in the past.
